note: Right for raw UDP datagrams (no delivery guarantee). But UDP is also the base for reliable transports: QUIC (RFC 9000, used by HTTP/3) carries its packets in UDP datagrams and adds the feedback needed for reliable delivery and congestion control. So 'UDP' alone doesn't mean 'drops data'; it means the reliability must be built above it.

The design intent (validate up front so the async write never fails for a business reason) is sound, but with Kafka consumers a crash after processing and before committing the offset means records get reprocessed (at-least-once). The persisting worker must therefore make the insert idempotent (e.g. keyed by message id); otherwise a redelivery produces exactly the duplicate-key failure or a duplicate row.
precise_version: Messages, once accepted, will always be persisted; the persisting consumer must make inserts idempotent because Kafka may redeliver after a crash.

Vector clocks do not give a 'true' total order: they give a partial causal order (one counter per participant), so they can tell that one message happened-before another or that two were concurrent, but concurrent messages still need a tie-break rule to be displayed in one order.
